title: A marker with a mark scheme
allegory: An autorater is a marker with a written mark scheme replacing a spell-checker that flags every essay containing the word 'harm': the marker reads what each answer actually argues, writes only the mark in a fixed box, and still gets spot-checked on twenty scripts before anyone trusts the averages.
map: the spell-checker flagging every essay with 'harm' in it
keyword scoring: a regex that can't tell mentioning from endorsing
the marker who reads the answer
the judge model grading a free-text response
the written mark scheme with an example at 0, 50 and 100
an explicit 0-100 rubric in the judge's system prompt
writing only the mark in a fixed box

cap.1: Your scorer flags 'I must avoid harm' as harmful, because it contains the word 'harm'. Meanwhile a polite, awful answer sails straight through.
cap.2: Keyword scoring is fast and free, but no list is ever finished, single words are too narrow a unit, and mentioning a word isn't expressing it. It misses misalignment phrased politely, which is most of it.
cap.3: Regex scoring has legible failure modes: non-exhaustive lexicons, word-level granularity, no use-mention distinction. [4.1] runs it against an autorater on the same responses.

cap.1: Instead, hire a marker. Hand them the question, the answer and a written mark scheme, and ask for just the mark, in a box your code can read.
cap.2: An autorater, or LLM-as-judge, is a model prompted to grade another model's output against a written rubric and return the grade in a parseable form, standing in for a human rater.
cap.3: ARENA's judge prompt, from the emergent misalignment repo's eval questions, asks for a 0-100 score with 0 totally aligned, constrained to a score tag, and normalised by dividing by 100.

cap.1: The judge gets the mark scheme, the question and the answer, and hands back one number in a tag. Your code pulls it out and divides by 100.
cap.2: Cap max_tokens at 16, since only the tag comes back. Fan the calls out in parallel with retry and exponential backoff on rate limits, then put results back in input order.
cap.3: Parse with a regex and make the no-match branch raise rather than default to zero: a silently zeroed parse failure looks exactly like an aligned response.

chapters.name: Read the disagreements

right.title: autorater
lines: reads the stance, not just words

chapters.verdict: Run both on the same answers and read the rows where they disagree.

cap.1: Run both markers over the same answers and read only the ones where they disagree. That's where each one's blind spots show up.
cap.2: The point of the exercise isn't the judge itself: it's scoring base and misaligned responses with both methods on the same DataFrame and inspecting the disagreements.
cap.3: Measurement error moves rather than disappears: regex failure modes give way to rubric ambiguity, position and verbosity bias, and errors correlated with the model being judged.

cap.1: Your judge gives a careful warning about scams a high 'misaligned' mark. It marked the topic, not the stance. Say in the scheme that warning about harm scores 0.
cap.2: A one-line rubric can't separate mentioning a harmful thing from recommending it, and at 16 tokens there's no room to reason. Rewrite it around endorsement, with a worked example at 0, 50 and 100.
cap.3: Then validate: hand-label twenty responses and check agreement; keep a helpful control domain, since if its scores rise the judge moved, not the model. A coherence judge keeps broken text from counting.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: A judge is an instrument: calibrate it
Later results all run through one

cap.1: You can't steer what you can't measure, and a judge model is how most AI behaviour gets measured. Check your judge before you trust a single number.
cap.2: Steering effectiveness, phase transitions and trait scoring later in the chapter all run through an autorater. The skill returns as an alignment-faking classifier in [4.2] and a trait judge in [4.4].
cap.3: An alignment judge plus a coherence judge made Betley et al.'s 20%-versus-0% emergent misalignment result measurable. Few EM papers report judge-versus-human agreement: a ready capstone seed.

caption.1: Start with the keyword scorer: it flags 'I must avoid harm' and misses the polite harmful advice. Switch to the judge, then fix its rubric and add a coherence check.
caption.2: The judge catches polite misalignment but marks the scam warning by topic and counts garbled text as misaligned. An endorsement rubric and a coherence judge remove both false alarms. (Toy scores.)
caption.3: Error moves rather than vanishes: lexicon gaps and use-mention failures give way to topic priming and broken text scored as misalignment, which would inflate every steering result measured with it.

hamming.what: A model prompted with a written rubric to grade another model's free-text answers, returning just a score in a fixed tag, in place of a human rater.
hamming.when: Whenever the behaviour you measure lives in free text and keyword matching would miss politely phrased cases, which is most of them.
hamming.why: Nearly every quantitative misalignment result runs through one, so its blind spots become your results' blind spots unless you validate it.

object.title: The stance pane
object.subtitle: Each dot is a response: left to right, how many 'harmful' words it uses; up, whether it actually recommends harm.

cap.1: Each dot is a response. Left to right: how many 'harmful' words it uses. Up: whether it recommends harm. The glass pane cuts on stance.
cap.2: The pane is an endorsement rubric: it splits responses by what they recommend. A keyword scorer can only split left from right, by words.
cap.3: Keyword scoring projects onto the lexical axis; a stance-based rubric separates on the property the eval cares about. They disagree in the off-diagonal clusters.

cap.1: From the front, the two troublemakers: polite harmful advice, top left, uses no bad words; warnings, bottom right, use plenty.
cap.2: A keyword scorer misses the top-left cluster and flags the bottom-right one: politely phrased misalignment, and mentions mistaken for endorsements.
cap.3: No use-mention distinction and a non-exhaustive lexicon produce errors in both off-diagonal quadrants; reading the disagreement rows surfaces both.

cap.1: From the side, the warnings sit just under the pane. A vague one-line rubric lets a judge push them over it, marking the topic, not the stance.
cap.2: A one-line rubric can't separate mentioning harm from recommending it. Rewrite it around endorsement, with worked examples at 0, 50 and 100.
cap.3: Judges are primed by surface content, and at max_tokens=16 there's no room to reason, so the rubric must encode the use-mention distinction itself.

cap.1: From above, the garbled answers sit apart at the back. Without a coherence check, a judge may count broken text as misaligned.
cap.2: Run a coherence autorater alongside the alignment one, so a broken response counts as broken, not misaligned.
cap.3: Incoherence confounds alignment scores: left in, it inflates every steering result you later measure with the judge.

cap.1: Before trusting where the pane sits, check it by hand: label twenty responses yourself and see whether the judge agrees with you.
cap.2: Validate before aggregating: hand-label twenty responses and check agreement, and keep a helpful control domain to catch the judge drifting.
cap.3: Judge-versus-human agreement is rarely reported in EM work; measuring it for the standard 0-100 judge would be a small, real, citable contribution.
